article.title: The Enshittification of Everyday Life
article.author: Jatinder Hayre
article.content: Have you tried to speak to a human being lately? Perhaps you wanted to question an energy bill, rearrange a hospital appointment, claim a benefit, or discover why your insurer had refused treatment your doctor said you needed. You will probably have been invited to download an app, create an account, and remember a password. The most recent demand is that you must interrogate a chatbot. And then, as a final act of administrative penance, you can telephone a call center, where a recorded voice assures you that your call is terribly important. Somewhere along the way, a strange inversion occurred: the institution still takes your money, increasingly so, but you perform more and more of the labor. This sort of scenario is usually called decline, but I think that is too generous. Decline suggests something tired, neglected, perhaps capable of rescue with another budget, or, more rarely, a sufficiently earnest politician. What we have instead is a deliberate paradigm shift. Cory Doctorow has a gloriously apt vulgarity for this: enshittification . Digital platforms court users with convenience, become indispensable, then worsen the bargain once leaving becomes harder than staying. You can delete Facebook. Try deleting your need for health care. Privatization and austerity have produced a miserable chimera: monopoly capitalism married to managerial bureaucracy. Government commissions, contractors deliver, regulators regulate, consultants advise, managers manage. Together they form the processariat : everybody owns a part of the process; nobody quite owns the responsibility. The exhausted receptionist absorbs the anger, while staffing and spending decisions are made in the ivory tower. Meanwhile, you are still on hold. This is “socialized inconvenience.” Once, institutions encountered complexity and employed people to deal with it; now they email the complexity to you. We photograph the meter, chase the referral, upload the evidence, and pursue which department has lost the form. Nevertheless, this is recorded as efficiency. Even the language has been enshittified: a closed desk becomes “digital transformation” and work transferred from salaried staff to unpaid customers becomes “empowerment.” Still, enshittification is subtler than collapse: things keep functioning, but with enough friction to render using them a second occupation. Your Call Is Important to Us As a practicing doctor, I see the more dangerous version. Being ill is work nobody pays you for: ringing at the right hour, decoding the letter, affording the fare, losing a day’s wages, explaining yourself again to somebody new. Patients increasingly become project managers of their own illnesses. The sicker the patient, the more administrative competence we seem to demand of them. The sickest people are often required to become the most capable bureaucrats. I remember one of my own patients who underwent a biopsy of a neck lump and was found to have cancer. The biopsy was performed, the pathology was reported and the result entered the system. Yet no appointment followed, no clinician called and nobody appeared to take responsibility for what happened next. My patient simply waited, assuming that somebody, somewhere, was dealing with it. Of course, cancer does not wait to consider mitigating circumstances. On paper, each step had occurred. In reality, the one thing that mattered had not: the patient had not been followed up with. Every part of the process can function while the person at the center of it is still failed. The American version comes with insurance paperwork. In a survey of 4,155 insured adults ages eighteen to sixty-four, 24.4 percent reported delaying or forgoing care because of administrative tasks. Respondents with disabilities reported greater burdens; those with higher incomes, fewer. They already had insurance. The affluent can often buy their way out of the processariat altogether: a private consultation instead of the appointment queue, a taxi instead of the disrupted train, a tutor instead of navigating a struggling school, an accountant or assistant instead of another afternoon lost to forms and hold music. Those without that option remain trapped inside the machinery and pay in the resource institutions almost never count: time. Forty minutes on hold is an irritation to somebody answering emails from home — to a care worker on an unpaid lunch break, it can mean abandoning the problem altogether. Money increasingly buys something subtler than luxury — an exit from process. In 2024, across twenty-eight OECD countries , the poorest fifth were, on average, 2.5 times more likely than the richest fifth to report unmet medical needs because of cost, distance, or waiting times. Chasing down a child’s appointment or a parent’s prescription requires human effort. The International Labour Organization’s 2018 report , drawing on sixty-four countries, estimated 16.4 billion hours of unpaid care work daily. Women performed 76.2 percent. Institutions shedding work rely on households already doing plenty. We empirically tested whether the effort and resources an intervention requires affect who benefits from it. Income support, housing measures and regulation produced the most consistent equity gains. Programs demanding sustained personal effort, without support, often widened health inequality. Giving everybody the same instructions does not give everybody the same capacity to act on them. When people give up asking, that can look like reduced demand, although the need has gone nowhere. Please Rate Your Health From One to Ten Arkansas made Medicaid coverage conditional on work and reporting requirements. By the time a judge halted the policy, eighteen thousand adults had lost coverage . Researchers found no employment increase over eighteen months. In Jharkhand, India, reforms introducing biometric identification for subsidized food reduced corruption, but an estimated 1.5 to 2 million legitimate beneficiaries lost access at some point during the reforms. The researchers traced much of the harm to how the transition was managed. Public ownership must mean enough staff with the authority to resolve problems. Universal entitlements must be obtainable without a second occupation spent pursuing them. The worker answering from another country has no more power over the staffing budget than the patient waiting. Both have an interest in changing who controls the service. And an institution claiming an efficiency saving should have to account for the work transferred to the public. Perhaps the most corrosive achievement of enshittification is our own habituation. We budget for the delay, expect the missed call and quietly absorb another piece of work the institution once did for us. What begins as irritation becomes adaptation. What once looked like failure is the new baseline. The processariat wins twice: first by making the service worse and then by persuading us that expecting better is somehow unreasonable. As we wait, chase, upload, appeal and telephone, the processariat can point to its dashboards and insist that the machinery is working. Broken institutions would at least have the decency to stop. Enshittified institutions keep going, largely because we have been conscripted into keeping them going ourselves. But at what cost?
